medical.title: Roadmap developed to strengthen surgical teamwork and patient safety
medical.summary: New research from University of Kentucky College of Medicine faculty member Helen Wei, M.D., Ph.D., assistant professor in acute care surgery, trauma and surgical critical care, is shedding light on the working relationship between surgeons and anesthesiologists. It's a critical but often overlooked factor in patient care.

medical.title: Heat wave effects can linger overnight in older adults, study finds
medical.summary: Cooling a home overnight may not be enough to protect older adults from the physiological effects of repeated daytime indoor overheating during a multiday heat wave, according to new research from the University of Ottawa.

medical.title: Decadelong study finds smoking worsens sickle cell retinopathy
medical.summary: Sickle cell retinopathy (SCR), a common, potentially blinding eye condition found among some people with sickle cell disease, is caused by misshapen blood cells blocking blood vessels in the light-sensing retina. In a 10-year retrospective study of adults with SCR treated at Wilmer Eye Institute, Johns Hopkins Medicine, researchers found active smoking is a strong modifiable risk factor for disease progression, highlighting smoking cessation and routine screening as two actionable means of preventing vision loss.

medical.title: Remote-control in the cortex—how distant synapses are equipped for change
medical.summary: The outermost layer of the brain's cerebral cortex is a major meeting point for information coming from across the brain. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research have now discovered that synapses in this thin layer can produce proteins locally. Published in Cell Reports, the study provides the first comprehensive molecular map of cortical layer 1 and its synapses, revealing a specialized signature and unexpected similarities with the hippocampus.

medical.title: Wearable stroke rehabilitation device gives patients the upper hand
medical.summary: A team led by University of Massachusetts Amherst researchers has developed a wearable wrist device powered by a machine-learning algorithm that can continuously track changes in arm movement impairment after a stroke. Monitoring those changes throughout rehabilitation could allow clinicians to adjust therapy in real time, tailoring care instead of relying on the current one-size-fits-all approach.

medical.title: Your voice may reveal how fast and how well you're aging
medical.summary: A large study shows that machine-learning clocks based on speech can estimate chronological age and may also offer a window into brain aging, biological aging, cognitive health, cumulative burden and dementia.

medical.title: How parenting profiles are associated with children's behavioral and emotional problems
medical.summary: There's no one right way to raise a child, but different patterns of parenting are associated with how kids behave. A new study, published in the PLOS One, identified data-driven profiles of parenting practices and investigated how they relate to children's behavioral and emotional problems. These are generally grouped into internalizing behaviors (e.g., withdrawal, anxiety, depression) and externalizing behaviors (e.g., aggression, oppositional behavior, attention problems).

medical.title: Newly uncovered enzyme mechanism could help target drug-resistant breast cancer
medical.summary: One of the major challenges in treating the most common subtype of breast cancer (hormone receptor positive, HR+) is the emergence of resistance to treatment. In a recent study, Boston Children's Hospital researchers and colleagues discovered a new driver of resistance, pointing to a way to detect resistant cancer cells early and a possible way to target them.

medical.title: Newly discovered cell recycling pathway unlocks the therapeutic potential of TFEB
medical.summary: For years, TFEB has been regarded as one of the most promising therapeutic targets for restoring the cell's ability to clear and recycle waste. Yet turning that promise into therapies has proved difficult because TFEB itself is hard to target with drugs. Now, a study published in Nature by scientists at the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) has identified a molecular pathway that controls TFEB activity, uncovering new druggable targets that could open the door to therapies for rare genetic diseases, cancer and other conditions linked to lysosomal dysfunction.

medical.title: Call for the WHO to declare the climate crisis a public health emergency of international concern
medical.summary: Researchers from Wits Planetary Health Research (Wits PHR), University of the Witwatersrand, and international partner institutions are calling on the World Health Organization (WHO) and its member states to formally declare the climate crisis a public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC), arguing that its immediate health impacts require a globally coordinated response to safeguard the health of the most vulnerable.

medical.title: 3D printing enables custom rubber gloves in smaller batches with less waste
medical.summary: Cranfield University researchers have developed a new method for 3D printing rubber gloves that is set to reshape the glove manufacturing industry.

medical.title: New AI platform could help cancer survivors get personalized support between doctor visits
medical.summary: Researchers with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, have created a framework for developing, evaluating and implementing AI tools in cancer survivorship and supportive care, according to a new proof-of-concept study published in the journal Translational Behavioral Medicine.

medical.title: Early findings suggest stimulating multiple brain regions could enrich artificial touch
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Osaka have shown that stimulating two parts of the brain at the same time may create richer artificial touch sensations. The study tested whether simultaneously stimulating the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and the insular cortex could produce sensations beyond the tingling or numbness typically elicited by S1 stimulation. The study is published in Brain Stimulation.

medical.title: Case report highlights multidisciplinary approach to recurrent prostate cancer
medical.summary: A case report led by UCLA Health researchers highlights the importance of a multidisciplinary, evidence-based approach to treating prostate cancer that returns after surgery, particularly when the disease recurs multiple times and in different locations.

medical.title: Experimental obesity drug targets appetite through amylin, offering potential alternative to GLP-1 therapies
medical.summary: New research presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy (Sept. 28–Oct. 2), and published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology shows that weekly injections of the new amylin-based obesity drug petrelintide can enable those treated to lose more than 10% of their body weight—generally less weight loss than with existing incretin-based (GLP-1 RA) drugs, but also with far fewer side effects.

medical.title: Language patterns during memory tests may reveal early cognitive dysfunction
medical.summary: Clinicians and researchers use standardized tests to assess memory and thinking ability. In one commonly used memory test, a short story is read to patients, and then they try to recall it from memory. Their responses are scored by counting the number of story details each patient remembers. However, this scoring ignores a wealth of information about how the person responded, such as the use of complex or simple sentences, repetition of story details or admissions that they forgot pieces of the story with comments such as "I forgot her name."

medical.title: Lung cancers can use two different mechanisms to evade KRAS-inhibiting drugs
medical.summary: About 25% of lung adenocarcinomas have mutations of the gene KRAS, which drives uncontrolled cell growth. In recent years, the FDA has approved two KRAS inhibitors to treat patients with KRAS mutations. While these drugs can work well initially, tumors almost always develop resistance to them.

medical.title: Setting the brain's internal clock: Single neuron type enables learning of motor timing
medical.summary: Whether speaking, driving or playing an instrument, nearly everything we do requires precise control over the timing of our actions. When we learn new skills, we must learn not only what movements to make but how to time them precisely.

medical.title: Family physicians lack formal, consistent menopause care training
medical.summary: Many family physicians care for women throughout their lives, yet little is known about the menopause education they receive during training. A new study suggests that, although menopause education is broadly incorporated into U.S. family medicine residency training programs today, content coverage is variable and training programs lack formal assessments. Results of the study are published online today in Menopause.

medical.title: Higher GLP-1 costs lead to lower adherence
medical.summary: Semaglutides, or GLP-1s, can produce substantial weight loss if individuals adhere to their doctor's instructions. But a new study from the University of Georgia suggests patients aren't taking the weight loss medication as prescribed, often because of high out-of-pocket costs.

medical.title: Game on: Collaboration brings art, technology and play to young neurology patients
medical.summary: For children participating in a six-minute walk test at the University of Kentucky, a trip down the clinic hallway can now become something more: a game.

medical.title: Machine learning toolkit can improve odds of drug development success
medical.summary: Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) is using a generative artificial intelligence (AI) tool to improve pharmaceutical development outcomes. The SwRI-developed GAMES, or Generative Approaches for Molecular Encodings, uses large language models (LLMs) to produce text strings representing chemical structures.

medical.title: Activating 'energy saver' mode significantly extends lives of animals in preclinical study
medical.summary: Scientists have successfully used a drug to prolong the lifespan of several species of animals, in some cases by more than 25%. The study, published in Aging Cell, found strong evidence that activating a protein that governs energy levels may help organisms live significantly longer.

medical.title: Getting their steps in: Preschoolers walk 18,000 steps a day
medical.summary: Children ages 3 and 4 take a median of 18,542 steps a day, but their daily step counts vary widely, according to the first international reference values for daily step counts in preschool-age children, published in the journal The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health.

medical.title: The dawn of the age of the exoskeleton
medical.summary: This year, members of Seattle Mountain Rescue have been setting off into the wilds of the U.S. Pacific Northwest wearing an unusual piece of equipment.

science.title: Mysterious oarfish's fins inspire large underwater robot design
science.summary: When designing a large underwater robot that could swim silently to avoid startling sea creatures, roboticist Rob Shepherd considered the unusual swimming system of oarfish, the meters-long fish whose ribbon-like dorsal fin moves in waves to propel its body.

science.title: How sea squirts perceive underwater noise
science.summary: Shipping, construction work and other human activities are altering the acoustic conditions in our planet's seas. Sound pressure is often examined to determine the effects that this underwater noise has on marine organisms. However, these observations may not be thorough enough for creatures that live on the seafloor.

science.title: International study identifies key childhood experiences that predict happiness and well-being in adulthood
science.summary: A new study, led by the University of Nottingham and conducted across three countries, has identified a set of key childhood experiences that predict multiple measures of well-being in adulthood—including health, happiness, anxiety, life satisfaction, satisfaction with social relationships and general trust in others.

science.title: Women leave psychology research more often than men, especially early in their careers
science.summary: Today, women are more likely than men to begin an academic career in psychology. Nevertheless, they leave research substantially more often, particularly during the first years after entering the field.

science.title: Chlamydia packs DNA with lipids, revealing possible target for blocking infection
science.summary: The bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis is one of the most common causes of sexually transmitted infections worldwide. Biologically, it is regarded as a highly specialized "nutrient thief": Because chlamydia have lost the ability to reproduce independently outside a host cell, they hijack human metabolic products—particularly sphingolipids—for their own development. Within the host cell, they create a sheltered environment known as an inclusion. These bacterial colonies often grow so large that they exceed the size of the human host cell's nucleus.

science.title: Poverty in the EU declined in the last decade, but disparities persist among nations
science.summary: Despite differences among nations, poverty in the European Union declined between 2015 and 2023, according to a study published in PLOS One by Silvia Megyesiova and Cecilia Olexova of the Bratislava University of Economics and Business in Košice, Slovak Republic.

science.title: Adult fossil strengthens evidence for Homo erectus in southern Africa 2 million years ago
science.summary: La Trobe archaeologists have described 18 new hominin fossils, including a second Homo erectus skull fragment that confirms the species first appeared in southern Africa 2.0 million years ago—200,000 years earlier than traditionally thought.

science.title: Star Trails
science.summary: This long-duration image shows star trails above Earth and the blue lights of fishing boats and the yellow lights of Indonesian cities stretching below the International Space Station as it orbited 258 miles above the Banda Sea on Sept. 20, 2026. Image credit: NASA/Anil Menon

science.title: 3D light fields push electrons into quantum states previously beyond experimental reach
science.summary: By superimposing two ultrashort laser pulses that converge from different directions, a team of physicists at the University of Oldenburg has succeeded in generating three-dimensional light fields.

science.title: Why the nor'easter's storm surge was so high, and what it says about the El Niño winter ahead
science.summary: As a powerful nor'easter hit the U.S. Atlantic coast in late September 2026, the ocean poured into coastal neighborhoods from North Carolina to New York. Water from the storm surge and heavy rain filled streets and surrounded homes as near-hurricane-force winds knocked out power. It may have even uncovered a shipwreck more than a century old.

science.title: Honeybee silk could power smarter wound dressings
science.summary: Biodegradable films made from engineered honeybee silk could form the basis of a new generation of "smart" wound dressings, according to researchers at CSIRO and Adelaide University.

science.title: Hidden star cluster discovered in Milky Way's crowded disk defies easy classification
science.summary: Astronomers have discovered a stellar cluster hidden in the crowded disk of the Milky Way. The object, named Garro 04, was first identified as an unusual collection of stars in observations from the VVVX survey and was later confirmed using infrared spectroscopy. A paper outlining the properties of this seemingly mysterious stellar system was posted to the arXiv preprint server on September 21.

science.title: Using an AI chatbot to practice new languages can be helpful, but it doesn't replace speaking with an actual person
science.summary: Approximately 30% of U.S. adults who were learning a language in 2025 reported that they were using artificial intelligence as a resource.

science.title: Sugar found in meteorites may have helped secure its own survival on early Earth
science.summary: Is there life elsewhere, or is Earth unique in the universe? This is one of humanity's great unanswered questions. One way to approach this mystery is to investigate how life began here on Earth. Our research explores the conditions in which a mixture of molecules somehow transformed from chemistry into biology.

science.title: Stoicism isn't just for men—despite what the manosphere suggests
science.summary: Stoicism has attracted all sorts of fans in recent years, but one group whose interest in this ancient philosophy has attracted a good deal of comment is the "manosphere."

science.title: Earth and Mars: Built from different cosmic recipes
science.summary: Four and a half billion years ago, Earth and Mars were born in the rotating cloud of gas and dust that would eventually become our solar system. Yet exactly how the planets formed remains one of the most disputed questions in planetary science.

science.title: Alpine bacteria show unexpected ability to fight viruses
science.summary: A silent, long-running competition has been taking place in Swiss alpine lakes for millions of years, killing trillions of organisms every day without anyone noticing. This competition between bacteria and viruses pushes both into a relentless evolutionary battle.

science.title: Drones, satellites and AI help scientists watch over Antarctica's smallest lifeforms
science.summary: Monitoring Antarctica's tiny, scattered ecosystems is a challenge that has long plagued researchers. But a new study led by the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new approach to tracking life in one of the most remote environments on Earth. The research is published in the ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing.

science.title: Light-activated crystals break down DNA-like molecules in water, potentially curbing antibiotic resistance
science.summary: Engineers have developed a new approach for turning ordinary water into a weapon against antibiotic-resistant bacteria, according to a study published in the journal Chem Catalysis.

science.title: Asgard archaea suggest crawling motility may be far older than previously thought
science.summary: Asgard archaea, our closest known microbial relatives, play a key role in current models of the origin of more complex organisms, known as eukaryotes (all animals, plants, protists and fungi). However, their biology has so far been poorly understood.

science.title: Little-studied Antarctic basin could raise sea levels, but melt timing remains unknown
science.summary: Over a century ago, Australian geologist Sir Douglas Mawson led a sledding expedition over hundreds of kilometers of ice into a remote part of East Antarctica. The party turned back after the tragic death of a party member. Fellow Australian Cecil Madigan led another group across sea ice into the region before also turning back.

science.title: Physicists identify 'octupolar' magnetism, with implications for quantum technologies
science.summary: Most magnets have two poles: north and south, or positive and negative, in a familiar arrangement called a "dipole." But researchers are increasingly uncovering more complex forms of magnetism.

science.title: Study: Paid internships deliver strong payoff early in careers
science.summary: A new national study co-authored by UW–Madison School of Education professor Mindi Thompson, who directs the university's Center for Research on College‑Workforce Transitions (CCWT), offers evidence that paid internships give college graduates a lasting advantage in earnings, job quality and early career progression.

science.title: A record-breaking X-ray flash may reveal the birth of a magnetar
science.summary: Astronomers have found strong evidence that some mysterious, minutes-long X-ray flashes are produced when two neutron stars collide and create a magnetar. One record-setting event glowed in X-rays for nearly 10 minutes, potentially opening a new way to find these extreme cosmic mergers.

science.title: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover finds groundwater, lakes, and hot fluids in one place
science.summary: NASA’s Perseverance rover has uncovered a surprisingly complicated history of water in Jezero Crater. Scientists expected the crater’s Margin Unit to contain lake sediments, but instead found ancient igneous rocks that were altered by water on at least three separate occasions.

environment.title: Ebola, twins and women-led conservation: Reporting on gorillas for World Gorilla Day
environment.summary: Gorillas are among humans’ closest relatives, with a common ancestor dating back around 8 to 10 million years. Both species of gorilla alive today are on the edge of extinction: The eastern gorilla (Gorilla beringei) is listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List, while the western gorilla (Gorilla gorilla) is critically endangered. In its […]

environment.title: In Nepal, women seek ownership rights to the lands they tend
environment.summary: POKHARA, Nepal — Before Binita Bishwokaarma understood Nepal’s property laws, she understood the work required to sustain a farm. Growing up in the village of Sindhupalchok, east of the capital, Kathmandu, she spent much of her time helping her mother around the house and in the fields while her father worked in the city. It’s […]

environment.title: New report reveals the environmental cost of USAID’s destruction
environment.summary: Nearly two years after U.S. President Trump’s decision to dismantle international development agency USAID removed nearly $1 billion from global conservation and environment funding, the agency’s absence is being felt across the world, new analysis says. The abrupt termination of around 5,200 contracts in early 2025 ended support for activities as varied as plastic waste […]

environment.title: ‘Lost’ bird reappears in West Africa’s forests after more than a decade
environment.summary: When Paulo Ditzel first laid eyes on the bird, he knew he’d seen something special: a vibrant orange body with yellow and black wings and tail feathers, topped by a dark head set off by almost-whimsical splashes of copper on its cheek. “My brain registered, it’s the Ghana cuckooshrike,” Ditzel, a field research fellow with […]

environment.title: Biodiversity credits shouldn’t copy the carbon market playbook (commentary)
environment.summary: Here is the argument I want to make plainly, before anything else: the biodiversity credit market should stop trying to copy carbon’s trick of reducing everything to one tradable unit, and should instead measure its own success by how continuously and independently a claim can be verified. Chasing a single elegant number, the way carbon […]

environment.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
environment.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

environment.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
environment.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

environment.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
environment.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

environment.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
environment.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

environment.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
environment.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

environment.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
environment.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

environment.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
environment.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.

environment.title: A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific
environment.summary: The Pacific was buzzing with storms while the Atlantic was notably quiet. The post A Trio of Tropical Cyclones in the Pacific appeared first on NASA Science .

mix_items.summary: When designing a large underwater robot that could swim silently to avoid startling sea creatures, roboticist Rob Shepherd considered the unusual swimming system of oarfish, the meters-long fish whose ribbon-like dorsal fin moves in waves to propel its body.

mix_items.title: Roadmap developed to strengthen surgical teamwork and patient safety
mix_items.summary: New research from University of Kentucky College of Medicine faculty member Helen Wei, M.D., Ph.D., assistant professor in acute care surgery, trauma and surgical critical care, is shedding light on the working relationship between surgeons and anesthesiologists. It's a critical but often overlooked factor in patient care.

mix_items.title: Heat wave effects can linger overnight in older adults, study finds
mix_items.summary: Cooling a home overnight may not be enough to protect older adults from the physiological effects of repeated daytime indoor overheating during a multiday heat wave, according to new research from the University of Ottawa.

mix_items.title: How sea squirts perceive underwater noise
mix_items.summary: Shipping, construction work and other human activities are altering the acoustic conditions in our planet's seas. Sound pressure is often examined to determine the effects that this underwater noise has on marine organisms. However, these observations may not be thorough enough for creatures that live on the seafloor.

mix_items.title: International study identifies key childhood experiences that predict happiness and well-being in adulthood
mix_items.summary: A new study, led by the University of Nottingham and conducted across three countries, has identified a set of key childhood experiences that predict multiple measures of well-being in adulthood—including health, happiness, anxiety, life satisfaction, satisfaction with social relationships and general trust in others.

mix_items.title: Women leave psychology research more often than men, especially early in their careers
mix_items.summary: Today, women are more likely than men to begin an academic career in psychology. Nevertheless, they leave research substantially more often, particularly during the first years after entering the field.

mix_items.title: Decadelong study finds smoking worsens sickle cell retinopathy
mix_items.summary: Sickle cell retinopathy (SCR), a common, potentially blinding eye condition found among some people with sickle cell disease, is caused by misshapen blood cells blocking blood vessels in the light-sensing retina. In a 10-year retrospective study of adults with SCR treated at Wilmer Eye Institute, Johns Hopkins Medicine, researchers found active smoking is a strong modifiable risk factor for disease progression, highlighting smoking cessation and routine screening as two actionable means of preventing vision loss.

mix_items.title: Remote-control in the cortex—how distant synapses are equipped for change
mix_items.summary: The outermost layer of the brain's cerebral cortex is a major meeting point for information coming from across the brain. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research have now discovered that synapses in this thin layer can produce proteins locally. Published in Cell Reports, the study provides the first comprehensive molecular map of cortical layer 1 and its synapses, revealing a specialized signature and unexpected similarities with the hippocampus.

mix_items.title: Chlamydia packs DNA with lipids, revealing possible target for blocking infection
mix_items.summary: The bacterium Chlamydia trachomatis is one of the most common causes of sexually transmitted infections worldwide. Biologically, it is regarded as a highly specialized "nutrient thief": Because chlamydia have lost the ability to reproduce independently outside a host cell, they hijack human metabolic products—particularly sphingolipids—for their own development. Within the host cell, they create a sheltered environment known as an inclusion. These bacterial colonies often grow so large that they exceed the size of the human host cell's nucleus.

mix_items.title: Wearable stroke rehabilitation device gives patients the upper hand
mix_items.summary: A team led by University of Massachusetts Amherst researchers has developed a wearable wrist device powered by a machine-learning algorithm that can continuously track changes in arm movement impairment after a stroke. Monitoring those changes throughout rehabilitation could allow clinicians to adjust therapy in real time, tailoring care instead of relying on the current one-size-fits-all approach.

mix_items.title: Your voice may reveal how fast and how well you're aging
mix_items.summary: A large study shows that machine-learning clocks based on speech can estimate chronological age and may also offer a window into brain aging, biological aging, cognitive health, cumulative burden and dementia.

mix_items.title: How parenting profiles are associated with children's behavioral and emotional problems
mix_items.summary: There's no one right way to raise a child, but different patterns of parenting are associated with how kids behave. A new study, published in the PLOS One, identified data-driven profiles of parenting practices and investigated how they relate to children's behavioral and emotional problems. These are generally grouped into internalizing behaviors (e.g., withdrawal, anxiety, depression) and externalizing behaviors (e.g., aggression, oppositional behavior, attention problems).

mix_items.title: Poverty in the EU declined in the last decade, but disparities persist among nations
mix_items.summary: Despite differences among nations, poverty in the European Union declined between 2015 and 2023, according to a study published in PLOS One by Silvia Megyesiova and Cecilia Olexova of the Bratislava University of Economics and Business in Košice, Slovak Republic.

mix_items.title: Newly uncovered enzyme mechanism could help target drug-resistant breast cancer
mix_items.summary: One of the major challenges in treating the most common subtype of breast cancer (hormone receptor positive, HR+) is the emergence of resistance to treatment. In a recent study, Boston Children's Hospital researchers and colleagues discovered a new driver of resistance, pointing to a way to detect resistant cancer cells early and a possible way to target them.

mix_items.title: Adult fossil strengthens evidence for Homo erectus in southern Africa 2 million years ago
mix_items.summary: La Trobe archaeologists have described 18 new hominin fossils, including a second Homo erectus skull fragment that confirms the species first appeared in southern Africa 2.0 million years ago—200,000 years earlier than traditionally thought.

mix_items.title: Star Trails
mix_items.summary: This long-duration image shows star trails above Earth and the blue lights of fishing boats and the yellow lights of Indonesian cities stretching below the International Space Station as it orbited 258 miles above the Banda Sea on Sept. 20, 2026. Image credit: NASA/Anil Menon

mix_items.title: Newly discovered cell recycling pathway unlocks the therapeutic potential of TFEB
mix_items.summary: For years, TFEB has been regarded as one of the most promising therapeutic targets for restoring the cell's ability to clear and recycle waste. Yet turning that promise into therapies has proved difficult because TFEB itself is hard to target with drugs. Now, a study published in Nature by scientists at the Telethon Institute of Genetics and Medicine (TIGEM) has identified a molecular pathway that controls TFEB activity, uncovering new druggable targets that could open the door to therapies for rare genetic diseases, cancer and other conditions linked to lysosomal dysfunction.

mix_items.title: 3D light fields push electrons into quantum states previously beyond experimental reach
mix_items.summary: By superimposing two ultrashort laser pulses that converge from different directions, a team of physicists at the University of Oldenburg has succeeded in generating three-dimensional light fields.

mix_items.title: Why the nor'easter's storm surge was so high, and what it says about the El Niño winter ahead
mix_items.summary: As a powerful nor'easter hit the U.S. Atlantic coast in late September 2026, the ocean poured into coastal neighborhoods from North Carolina to New York. Water from the storm surge and heavy rain filled streets and surrounded homes as near-hurricane-force winds knocked out power. It may have even uncovered a shipwreck more than a century old.

mix_items.title: Call for the WHO to declare the climate crisis a public health emergency of international concern
mix_items.summary: Researchers from Wits Planetary Health Research (Wits PHR), University of the Witwatersrand, and international partner institutions are calling on the World Health Organization (WHO) and its member states to formally declare the climate crisis a public health emergency of international concern (PHEIC), arguing that its immediate health impacts require a globally coordinated response to safeguard the health of the most vulnerable.

mix_items.title: 3D printing enables custom rubber gloves in smaller batches with less waste
mix_items.summary: Cranfield University researchers have developed a new method for 3D printing rubber gloves that is set to reshape the glove manufacturing industry.

mix_items.title: New AI platform could help cancer survivors get personalized support between doctor visits
mix_items.summary: Researchers with Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, part of the University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, have created a framework for developing, evaluating and implementing AI tools in cancer survivorship and supportive care, according to a new proof-of-concept study published in the journal Translational Behavioral Medicine.

mix_items.title: Early findings suggest stimulating multiple brain regions could enrich artificial touch
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Osaka have shown that stimulating two parts of the brain at the same time may create richer artificial touch sensations. The study tested whether simultaneously stimulating the primary somatosensory cortex (S1) and the insular cortex could produce sensations beyond the tingling or numbness typically elicited by S1 stimulation. The study is published in Brain Stimulation.

mix_items.title: Case report highlights multidisciplinary approach to recurrent prostate cancer
mix_items.summary: A case report led by UCLA Health researchers highlights the importance of a multidisciplinary, evidence-based approach to treating prostate cancer that returns after surgery, particularly when the disease recurs multiple times and in different locations.

mix_items.title: Experimental obesity drug targets appetite through amylin, offering potential alternative to GLP-1 therapies
mix_items.summary: New research presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) in Milan, Italy (Sept. 28–Oct. 2), and published in The Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology shows that weekly injections of the new amylin-based obesity drug petrelintide can enable those treated to lose more than 10% of their body weight—generally less weight loss than with existing incretin-based (GLP-1 RA) drugs, but also with far fewer side effects.

mix_items.title: Honeybee silk could power smarter wound dressings
mix_items.summary: Biodegradable films made from engineered honeybee silk could form the basis of a new generation of "smart" wound dressings, according to researchers at CSIRO and Adelaide University.

mix_items.title: Hidden star cluster discovered in Milky Way's crowded disk defies easy classification
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have discovered a stellar cluster hidden in the crowded disk of the Milky Way. The object, named Garro 04, was first identified as an unusual collection of stars in observations from the VVVX survey and was later confirmed using infrared spectroscopy. A paper outlining the properties of this seemingly mysterious stellar system was posted to the arXiv preprint server on September 21.

mix_items.title: Using an AI chatbot to practice new languages can be helpful, but it doesn't replace speaking with an actual person
mix_items.summary: Approximately 30% of U.S. adults who were learning a language in 2025 reported that they were using artificial intelligence as a resource.

mix_items.title: Language patterns during memory tests may reveal early cognitive dysfunction
mix_items.summary: Clinicians and researchers use standardized tests to assess memory and thinking ability. In one commonly used memory test, a short story is read to patients, and then they try to recall it from memory. Their responses are scored by counting the number of story details each patient remembers. However, this scoring ignores a wealth of information about how the person responded, such as the use of complex or simple sentences, repetition of story details or admissions that they forgot pieces of the story with comments such as "I forgot her name."

mix_items.title: Lung cancers can use two different mechanisms to evade KRAS-inhibiting drugs
mix_items.summary: About 25% of lung adenocarcinomas have mutations of the gene KRAS, which drives uncontrolled cell growth. In recent years, the FDA has approved two KRAS inhibitors to treat patients with KRAS mutations. While these drugs can work well initially, tumors almost always develop resistance to them.

mix_items.title: Setting the brain's internal clock: Single neuron type enables learning of motor timing
mix_items.summary: Whether speaking, driving or playing an instrument, nearly everything we do requires precise control over the timing of our actions. When we learn new skills, we must learn not only what movements to make but how to time them precisely.

mix_items.title: Family physicians lack formal, consistent menopause care training
mix_items.summary: Many family physicians care for women throughout their lives, yet little is known about the menopause education they receive during training. A new study suggests that, although menopause education is broadly incorporated into U.S. family medicine residency training programs today, content coverage is variable and training programs lack formal assessments. Results of the study are published online today in Menopause.

mix_items.title: Sugar found in meteorites may have helped secure its own survival on early Earth
mix_items.summary: Is there life elsewhere, or is Earth unique in the universe? This is one of humanity's great unanswered questions. One way to approach this mystery is to investigate how life began here on Earth. Our research explores the conditions in which a mixture of molecules somehow transformed from chemistry into biology.

mix_items.title: Stoicism isn't just for men—despite what the manosphere suggests
mix_items.summary: Stoicism has attracted all sorts of fans in recent years, but one group whose interest in this ancient philosophy has attracted a good deal of comment is the "manosphere."

mix_items.title: Higher GLP-1 costs lead to lower adherence
mix_items.summary: Semaglutides, or GLP-1s, can produce substantial weight loss if individuals adhere to their doctor's instructions. But a new study from the University of Georgia suggests patients aren't taking the weight loss medication as prescribed, often because of high out-of-pocket costs.

mix_items.title: Game on: Collaboration brings art, technology and play to young neurology patients
mix_items.summary: For children participating in a six-minute walk test at the University of Kentucky, a trip down the clinic hallway can now become something more: a game.

mix_items.title: Earth and Mars: Built from different cosmic recipes
mix_items.summary: Four and a half billion years ago, Earth and Mars were born in the rotating cloud of gas and dust that would eventually become our solar system. Yet exactly how the planets formed remains one of the most disputed questions in planetary science.

mix_items.title: Machine learning toolkit can improve odds of drug development success
mix_items.summary: Southwest Research Institute (SwRI) is using a generative artificial intelligence (AI) tool to improve pharmaceutical development outcomes. The SwRI-developed GAMES, or Generative Approaches for Molecular Encodings, uses large language models (LLMs) to produce text strings representing chemical structures.

mix_items.title: Alpine bacteria show unexpected ability to fight viruses
mix_items.summary: A silent, long-running competition has been taking place in Swiss alpine lakes for millions of years, killing trillions of organisms every day without anyone noticing. This competition between bacteria and viruses pushes both into a relentless evolutionary battle.

mix_items.title: Activating 'energy saver' mode significantly extends lives of animals in preclinical study
mix_items.summary: Scientists have successfully used a drug to prolong the lifespan of several species of animals, in some cases by more than 25%. The study, published in Aging Cell, found strong evidence that activating a protein that governs energy levels may help organisms live significantly longer.

mix_items.title: Getting their steps in: Preschoolers walk 18,000 steps a day
mix_items.summary: Children ages 3 and 4 take a median of 18,542 steps a day, but their daily step counts vary widely, according to the first international reference values for daily step counts in preschool-age children, published in the journal The Lancet Child & Adolescent Health.

mix_items.title: Drones, satellites and AI help scientists watch over Antarctica's smallest lifeforms
mix_items.summary: Monitoring Antarctica's tiny, scattered ecosystems is a challenge that has long plagued researchers. But a new study led by the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new approach to tracking life in one of the most remote environments on Earth. The research is published in the ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing.

mix_items.title: The dawn of the age of the exoskeleton
mix_items.summary: This year, members of Seattle Mountain Rescue have been setting off into the wilds of the U.S. Pacific Northwest wearing an unusual piece of equipment.

mix_items.title: Light-activated crystals break down DNA-like molecules in water, potentially curbing antibiotic resistance
mix_items.summary: Engineers have developed a new approach for turning ordinary water into a weapon against antibiotic-resistant bacteria, according to a study published in the journal Chem Catalysis.

mix_items.title: Asgard archaea suggest crawling motility may be far older than previously thought
mix_items.summary: Asgard archaea, our closest known microbial relatives, play a key role in current models of the origin of more complex organisms, known as eukaryotes (all animals, plants, protists and fungi). However, their biology has so far been poorly understood.

mix_items.title: Little-studied Antarctic basin could raise sea levels, but melt timing remains unknown
mix_items.summary: Over a century ago, Australian geologist Sir Douglas Mawson led a sledding expedition over hundreds of kilometers of ice into a remote part of East Antarctica. The party turned back after the tragic death of a party member. Fellow Australian Cecil Madigan led another group across sea ice into the region before also turning back.

mix_items.title: Physicists identify 'octupolar' magnetism, with implications for quantum technologies
mix_items.summary: Most magnets have two poles: north and south, or positive and negative, in a familiar arrangement called a "dipole." But researchers are increasingly uncovering more complex forms of magnetism.

mix_items.title: Study: Paid internships deliver strong payoff early in careers
mix_items.summary: A new national study co-authored by UW–Madison School of Education professor Mindi Thompson, who directs the university's Center for Research on College‑Workforce Transitions (CCWT), offers evidence that paid internships give college graduates a lasting advantage in earnings, job quality and early career progression.

mix_items.title: A record-breaking X-ray flash may reveal the birth of a magnetar
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have found strong evidence that some mysterious, minutes-long X-ray flashes are produced when two neutron stars collide and create a magnetar. One record-setting event glowed in X-rays for nearly 10 minutes, potentially opening a new way to find these extreme cosmic mergers.

mix_items.title: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover finds groundwater, lakes, and hot fluids in one place
mix_items.summary: NASA’s Perseverance rover has uncovered a surprisingly complicated history of water in Jezero Crater. Scientists expected the crater’s Margin Unit to contain lake sediments, but instead found ancient igneous rocks that were altered by water on at least three separate occasions.

mix_items.title: Crocodiles are famous for finding their way home. These ones didn’t
mix_items.summary: Captive-raised saltwater crocodiles released into Bangladesh’s Sundarbans surprised scientists by settling into the wild rather than trying to return to their breeding facility. The result suggests that releasing larger, mature captive crocodiles could help restore depleted populations more successfully than relying only on vulnerable hatchlings.

mix_items.title: Back-to-back Arctic storms can double sea ice loss
mix_items.summary: Scientists have found that Arctic cyclones become especially destructive when several strike one after another. These storm clusters cause about twice as much sea ice loss as isolated cyclones, with impacts that persist roughly two and a half times longer. As Arctic ice becomes thinner and weaker, the damage from these storms appears to be increasing, potentially creating a feedback loop that accelerates future ice loss.

mix_items.title: Scientists finally see DNA “zip” itself together for the first time
mix_items.summary: Scientists have directly observed how two negatively charged DNA molecules can pair up despite normally repelling each other. Positively charged metal ions appear to bridge the gap, helping matching DNA helices align groove for groove like a molecular zipper. The discovery confirms a theory proposed two decades ago and could help researchers understand DNA interactions involved in cancer and other cellular processes.

mix_items.title: Have we found alien life? Hundreds of scientists weigh in
mix_items.summary: Two major alien-life announcements in 2025 generated enormous excitement, but most astrobiologists remained unconvinced. Only 6.6% of surveyed experts thought possible biological molecules on K2-18b probably represented extraterrestrial life, while 15.1% said the same about intriguing mineral patterns in a Martian rock.

mix_items.title: Devil’s Arrows: Ancient builders hauled 55,000-pound stones 11 miles for Britain’s tallest stone row
mix_items.summary: Britain’s towering Devil’s Arrows were built from 25-tonne stones hauled at least 18 kilometers from Brimham Rocks around 4,000 years ago. The discovery reveals an astonishing feat of prehistoric engineering and suggests the stones’ distant source may have been chosen for cultural or spiritual reasons.

mix_items.title: “Parachute science” is failing the tropics, home to more than 80% of insect species
mix_items.summary: Insects quietly hold much of the natural world together, yet conservation efforts are overlooking the tropical regions where more than 80 percent of insect species live. Monash University researchers have developed a global framework to close this gap by combining scientific studies with museum collections, local expertise, citizen science, social media records, and new technologies.

mix_items.title: Geologists reveal the Americas collided millions of years earlier than thought
mix_items.summary: Volcanic rocks in Colombia are rewriting the timeline of the collision between Central and South America. Their magnetic signatures show that major tectonic deformation had already weakened by the late Miocene, suggesting the most intense collision occurred earlier than previously believed.
